To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cold seeps are characterized by a diagnostic hydrocarbon-metazoan-microbe-carbonate association, which is the result of the interaction between fluid flux rates, fluid compositions and seep fauna.
seepage is the result of the interaction between the geosphere and the oceanic crust.
cold seeps are a manifestation of the interaction between geologic processes and biogeochemistry.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the geologic and geochemical controls on fluid composition, the environmental conditions at cold seeps, the biogeochemical reactions in cold seep sediments and the resulting geochemical and geobiological manifestations.
the biogeochemistry of the seafloor and its interaction with geologic settings, which in the long-term will help in understanding the role of the seafloors as a global methane sink and source.
understanding how the geosphere and the biosphere interact in the subseafloor to produce the seafloor manifestations we see today.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

seep fluids, their geochemistry and the seafloor manifestations are a result of the geology of the respective setting, the geologic age of the sediments and their organic matter content, the sedimentary environment, and the environmental conditions at the time of seepage, and that these are the most important criteria for seep characterization and environmental assessment.
the seep manifestations are the result of a complex interaction between the geological setting, the fluid composition and the biotic community.

seepage is a pervasive phenomenon at most convergent and transform margins, that it is controlled by the geologic setting and the composition of host sediments/rocks, but that the environmental impact and the global significance of seepage are not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
seafloor cold seeps are the most dynamic and diverse ecosystems on the ocean floor, but they are not a major sink for methane.
seep research has advanced from a descriptive to a process-oriented discipline, with the goal of understanding seepage as a process of the geosphere–ocean interface.
seeps at different settings are more alike than different, and that the differences are more subtle and less easily discerned than previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the seafloor is a dynamic interface of the Earth’s crust and mantle, which is continuously fed by volatile compounds and their carriers from depth.
seeps are a natural phenomenon that is not restricted to specific geotectonic settings.
cold seeps are a ubiquitous feature of convergent plate margins and that they are an important component of the carbon and sulfur cycles.
